text: Lesson 25 named network and routing, security group and NSG rules, and DNS as three of the five places a deployment usually breaks. This lesson turns those three, plus one more practical check, into one fixed, repeatable sequence you run on any connectivity ticket, in the same order, every single time, instead of chasing whatever layer your gut suspects first.

The first three questions move from broad to specific. Is the resource actually running at all? Is there a route from where the traffic originates to where the resource lives? And is the firewall, NSG, or security group actually allowing this exact traffic right now, not just something that looks related? Lesson 32's incident lived at question three — the rule existed, but its source range had gone stale.

The last two questions get more specific still. Does the hostname actually resolve to the IP you expect, confirmed with nslookup or dig? And is the service itself actually listening on the expected port, since a crashed or misconfigured app can refuse a connection even over a perfect network path. The sequence stops the moment any question fails — there's no reason to keep checking once you've found the answer.

Take a real ticket: can't connect to the app server on port 8080. The resource is running, and the route table shows a clean path to the internet gateway — both pass. But the NSG rule list shows no rule permitting port 8080 inbound at all. That's where the sequence stops, and that's the entire root cause: a missing rule, not a dead server or a bad route.

Working top to bottom instead of jumping straight to a hunch is exactly how Lesson 31's and Lesson 32's incidents both resolved in minutes instead of an hour of scattered guessing. Next, Lesson 27 covers the failure mode this sequence doesn't catch at all: tickets where the network was never the problem, and the real cause is a missing permission.
